speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MAINLAND CHINA-PROGRESS REPORT ON ESTABLISHING RELATIONS WITH PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to give a brief statement to the house about the government's progress in establishing relations with the People's Republic of China. Our embassy in Stockholm has been instructed to get in touch with the embassy of the People's Republic of China in order to convey the Canadian proposal that talks concerning relations between the two countries be held at a mutually convenient time and place in the near future. I hope that before long we shall have a reply from the Chinese government and that representatives of our two countries can then begin to discuss the question of recognition of the People's Republic of China and the exchange of embassies between Ottawa and Peking.
We also hope to be able to take this opportunity to explore with Chinese officials the whole range of Sino-Canadian relations, and to discuss the possibilities for expanding and developing our relations in a number of areas. Even without diplomatic relations, we have been able to develop our trade, exchange correspondents between Ottawa and Peking, and increase contacts between Canada and China in a number of fields in recent years.
There will be a number of questions for our officials to discuss with the Chinese. It is not only a question of working out a satisfactory basis for recognition and the exchange of embassies, but of reaching agreement on a number of details relating to the operations of a Canadian embassy in Peking and a Chinese embassy in Ottawa. Since these questions are
to be the subject of discussion, I do not think it would be appropriate to say any more about them now.

subsubtopic: MAINLAND CHINA-PROGRESS REPORT ON ESTABLISHING RELATIONS WITH PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC
speechtext:
First of all, Mr. Speaker, it is somewhat awkward to attempt to respond to a statement concerning the People's Republic of China without having notice, but I suppose members of parliament have been made aware, by statements, of the government's intentions in this regard. I would hope those countries of the world such as Italy, Belgium and Canada that are now engaged in serious negotiations with the People's Republic of China will be flexible enough so that the Nationalist government of China as represented in Taiwan will not by its action be outside the world community. However, presumably this would be a decision of the government of Taiwan and not a decision of the government of China.
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
Of course it is quite unrealistic for 700 million of the world's people to be outside the ordinary diplomatic exchanges among nations, and I think that anybody who has made a study of international matters feels that a change would have to be made, I personally hope the day will not be too far removed when the People's Republic of China can take its place as a member of the United Nations, because I believe that universality of membership in the United Nations is an objective that all countries should pursue.
Obviously the negotiations will take place in secret, but you know, Mr. Speaker, white papers do not have to be lengthy documents and it would be a help in a so-called participatory democracy if the government's intentions toward the People's Republic of China and the Nationalist government of China were made the subject of a white paper.

1. The federal-provincial conference of Ministers of Welfare, which is now being held annually, was convened to consider a number of problems of mutual interest in the social welfare field. Major attention was given to the Canada Assistance Plan. The ministers agreed to collaborate in a variety of activities aimed at making their welfare programs more effective, particularly as they affect disadvantaged and alienated persons. They agreed to set up a number of task forces, working groups, and intergovernmental committees to achieve these objectives. The question of Indian welfare was considered, and the Ministers of National Health and Welfare and of Indian Affairs and Northern Development repeated the federal government's offer to the provinces to share in the costs of welfare programs to ensure that Indians would receive the same level and quality of services provided to other residents of the province. It was agreed that continued negotiations would be held on this subject.
2.	The question of federal support to provincial legal aid programs was discussed, but no conclusions were reached. Further consideration will be given to this subject at future conferences. The question of the establishment of a national legal aid program was not discussed. If and when any action is taken in this matter, it will be announced to parliament in the usual manner.
3.	It was agreed that three study groups would be set up. The first will develop a

research program on alienation as it relates to social assistance recipients. The second will study the possibility of a developmental approach to public assistance, with the aim of directing the major public assistance programs toward the rehabilitation of those who have a potential for complete or partial selfsupport. A study will also be undertaken of cost factors in social assistance, with special attention being given to improved financial and statistical reporting and better methods of analyzing caseloads and the factors contributing to rising assistance costs.
The determination of the terms of reference and membership of these study groups is being worked out in collaboration with the provinces. Reports of the studies will be made to a conference of federal and provincial Ministers of Welfare.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF FRESHWATER FISH MARKETING CORPORATION
speechtext:
I rise to speak briefly on the third reading of Bill C-148, an act to regulate interprovincial and export trade in freshwater fish, and to establish the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation. It is my opinion that this particular act has received a thorough study by all concerned, at all stages of the bill.
The measure was first debated at the resolution stage under our old rules of procedure, and was given first reading on December 18, 1968. On January 16 the bill was again before
February 10, 1969
5324	COMMONS
Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation the house where it was thoroughly debated, given second reading and referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry. The standing committee met on Tuesday, January 28, a clause by clause study was carried out, and the bill as amended was reported to the house.
On Friday, February 7, the house again dealt with this measure at the report stage and members on this side of the house did their best to amend the legislation in order that the corporation, when opening its doors for business, might be truly representative of the people whom it was designed to serve. In this we were only partly successful, but the subamendment moved to our amendment by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Anderson) indicated a change of heart on the part of members supporting the government, and we believe the corporation will be better served by an advisory committee of 15 members, of whom at least one third should be persons or representatives of persons actively engaged in the freshwater fishing industry as fishermen.
It is unfortunate, in our view, that the government could not accept the suggestion that the Auditor General be appointed to carry out an annual audit of the accounts and financial transactions of the corporation. We took this stand because the bill does not indicate who will keep the books, who will be responsible for the preparation of financial statements or who is to be responsible for auditing the accounts of the corporation. The Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) has stated that in the end the Auditor General may well be the auditor appointed to audit the books of the corporation. However, his refusal to place this wording in the act raises some doubts in our minds concerning the person or persons who will ultimately be responsible for auditing the accounts of the corporation. After all, the Canadian taxpayer has a considerable stake in this corporation. It is to receive, initially, a grant of an amount not exceeding $100,000, with power to borrow up to five million dollars, backed up by the resources of the federal government, which really means by the people of Canada.
It is easy to understand our concern with regard to the responsibility for auditing the books of this corporation when one looks at some of the classic examples of mismanagement and improper estimating which have come to light recently. The increase in expenditures over estimates for the refitting of the Bonaventure, the increase in expenditures


over the estimates for the National Arts Centre, are staggering and they literally have the taxpayers of Canada hanging on the ropes.
When setting up this corporation we are dealing with an estimate, made by someone within the department, and we are told that a grant of $100,000 will enable the corporation to meet initial operating and establishment expenses. From experience of the examples to which I have referred, we have no way of knowing what the actual costs will be. We can only hope and pray that this estimate will be more accurate than estimates made in the past, since under clause 15 (1) the corporation is required to conduct its operations on a self-sustaining financial basis without appropriations therefor by parliament. If the initial estimate is too low, what happens to the corporation? Neither the bill nor the minister has been very clear on this point and I suggest it is one which he may wish to clarify.
The same question would apply to the amount which may be borrowed by the corporation, since the amount of any bank loans shall not exceed five million dollars. I presume this figure is also an estimate. I cannot help but wonder what would happen to the corporation if its total funds became tied up in property and in holding fish in storage to obtain higher prices. Certainly the fishermen could not come to its rescue, and I wonder whether the responsibility would not rest with the federal government or the provinces to provide more capital.
It is evident, Mr. Speaker, that under the terms of this all-encompassing legislation covering the buying, filleting, freezing, packaging and preparing of fish for market, high costs will be involved at the initial stage. The corporation, according to its purposes and powers, must not only buy and prepare fish but it must store, ship, insure, import, export, market, sell and otherwise dispose of fish and fish byproducts manufactured or produced by it. In addition it must establish branches or employ agents in Canada or elsewhere. It must make loans of working capital on a seasonal basis to persons engaged in fishing for commercial purposes in a participating province, and do all such other things as are necessary to the carrying out of any of its functions under the act. And it must do all these things, Mr. Speaker, on a capital grant of $100,000.
It seems to me that what we have before us is another faulty estimate. If this corporation is to carry out all the requirements of the freshwater fish industry I question the judgment of the man or men who made the initial
February 10, 1969	COMMONS
estimate covering the requirements of the board.
If the corporation can be established and become a successful, effective organization, providing better prices and services to inland fishermen, using the amounts as listed in this bill, the corporation will in my view have achieved its objective. There can be only one purpose for this corporation, and that is to provide some 7,000 inland fishermen in the vast area covering northern Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Northwest Territories with a better standard of living through a higher percentage return on the fish they catch. Under private enterprise, according to the Mclvor Committee report, fishermen received between 50 per cent and 60 per cent of the export price. These figures are known, so it will be up to the corporation to do better.
It will be the responsibility of the corporation to bring about an improvement in the bargaining position of our inland fishery, by co-ordinating supply and demand and by providing uniform standards and quality control. It will be the responsibility of the corporation to improve the quality of all the fish it places on the market, so that the consumer will have confidence in Canadian fresh water fish products.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
It will also be the responsibility of the corporation to co-ordinate the handling and processing of all freshwater fish; and, most important of all, it will be the corporation's responsibility to see that the hoped for higher export earnings will be passed on directly to the fishermen. In the final analysis it is the lone fisherman with whom we must be concerned. Unless his earnings are increased, unless he is given an opportunity to improve his status in the community, unless he is given a better income to provide for the needs of his family and for the education of his children, this whole exercise becomes one which only increases government bureaucracy, without providing any real assistance for the people it was designed to help.
Since the marketing board concept for an inland fishery is an entirely new departure- to the best of my knowledge, Mr. Speaker, this is the first time we have had a federal fresh fish marketing corporation in Canada-I cannot help but wonder what efforts are being made by all the governments concerned to acquaint fishermen who reside in this vast
DEBATES	5325
Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation area with the authority as well as the scope of the operations of the board.
In view of the marketing difficulties experienced by our fishermen, which in effect brought about the establishment of this marketing board, I cannot help but wonder whether the Canadian government has made a formal approach to the government of the United States to agree on a method of inspection of whitefish satisfactory to both governments. This is an important consideration at the initial stages of the setting up of this corporation. Apparently some 80 per cent of all our fish exported to the United States consists of whitefish. Since there is no standard inspection and since the whitefish at times are infected with a parasite, making the fish unacceptable to the United States authorities although that fish may be accepted by our Canadian authorities, I suggest to the government and the minister piloting this bill through the house that, if the freshwater fish corporation is to be successful, this is one area in which the government ought to consider taking action.
I wish to say that we, on this side, support this legislation. We hope, for the sake of the people in the vast area the corporation will serve, that the corporation will be successful in its operations.

Kon. Olio E. Lang (Saskaloon-Kumboldl) (for lhe Minisler of Industry, Trade and Commerce) moved second reading and reference to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs of Bill S-25, to amend the Export and Import Permits Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill to amend the Export and Import Permits Act is a fairly simple one. It extends for a further period legislation which has been in effect for a considerable period of time. Legislation in 1947 created the Export and Import Permits Act as a successor to the National Emergency Transitional Powers Act. Since 1954 the bill has been brought before the house at three-year intervals to be re-enacted in each case.
The re-enactment at this time is scheduled for a five-year period as against the three-year period previously used. It is our feeling there may well be merit in having re-enactment of this bill by each parliament. The three-year period could bring it back before the same parliament for a second time, which is undesirable. Accordingly, this amendment is for a longer period.
The only other change in substance is the inclusion of the Canadian Dairy Commission Act in the list of acts under which action may be taken. This is really a housekeeping matter since this change in the Export and Import Permits Act has already been made in the Canadian Dairy Commission Act.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
It is under this legislation that certain steps can be taken by the government in regard to some matters of export and import control. The export control may relate to such matters as arms and ammunition or may supplement certain other specific intergovernmental arrangements that have been entered into. The import controls are similarly designed, frequently to supplement other governmental action and particularly to supplement action where stabilization of price is being undertaken under some other legislation.
The purpose of the act is also to ensure that in certain cases goods which are of particular importance to Canada may not be exported outside Canada without regard to the interests of this country. Therefore the bill before us is a fairly simple continuation of the existing legislation, and I am pleased at this point to move its second reading and that it be referred to the appropriate committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the minister has indicated, this is essentially a housekeeping bill to provide for the extension of the legislation for a further period of five years. The extension to five years instead of the normal three years is not a matter to which anyone will take much objection.
Certainly the need for the extension of the legislation is quite manifest. As the minister has outlined, its chief purpose is to enable the government to impose import controls particularly so far as agricultural products are concerned, so that it will be possible to carry out the provisions of the Agricultural Stabilization Act, the Agricultural Products Cooperative Marketing Act, the Agricultural Products Board Act and the Fisheries Prices Support Act. To these is now to be added the Canadian Dairy Commission Act.
If that type of price stabilization is to work satisfactorily it is essential that the government have power to impose import controls on goods which would otherwise come in, undersell Canadian subsidized products and thus make the workings of our stabilization legislation ineffective. The chief point I would like to make in that connection is that I hope the government will be more active than it has been in the past in making use of this act. During the past four or five years the government has been very loath to use the act and put import controls into effect in cases where Canadian agricultural products were being damaged simply by the failure to use the provisions of the existing legislation. As a matter of fact, during that period some import controls were done away with. I recall that last year when poultry producers, particularly turkey producers, were in very considerable difficulties the government refused to take action and put import controls into effect. Speaking for this party I would say we are not only in favour of this legislation being renewed but that we are strongly in favour of it being used more effectively than has been the case in the past several years.
Dealing with the application of the act so far as export controls are concerned and the protection it provides, particularly with respect to the export of warlike material of any kind, I think that protection is manifestly necessary and nothing more needs to be said about it. The same applies so far as certain rare metals are concerned and metals which are in short supply from time to time. I anticipate that the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs when
February 10, 1969	COMMONS
examining the bill would like further information with regard to the extent to which the act is being made use of at present, and would like some expression of the intention of the government as to how effectively it will use it in the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are all interested in seeing this bill reach the standing committee where we can examine it in details. The bill involves a clear example of the kind of power possessed by governments but which is not used by them in certain cases where the national interest would be best served by doing so.
My party feels that the scope of the bill should be enlarged to cover all imports and all exports, rather than being confined to those specified in it. My reason for saying this is fairly straightforward. Quite obviously the reason that warlike materials and some agricultural products were included originally under the provisions of the act was that there existed an urgent need in those areas for the government to exercise control at some stage of their import and export. Even though in the past governments have been reluctant to act on these matters, they possessed the power to do so if the national interests or the interests of specific industries were in jeopardy. But by restricting this power to cover only certain items we run the risk of emergencies arising with respect to other items, and the government would not be able to act even if it wished to do so.
The legislative process is a lengthy one. It takes time to bring legislation before the house, to examine it and to pass it. There can be no other way to handle legislation in a democratic nation and this must be recognized. It is for this reason that we think the government should possess the power to act in case of emergencies with respect to other items.
With respect to import restrictions the provisions of the bill deal almost solely with agricultural products. I think it must be clear to many hon. members that there are other goods which stand in the same jeopardy as the agricultural products listed in the bill. My area of Waterloo has two major industries, a textile industry and a shoe industry, which from time to time are seriously jeopardized by imports from foreign countries. Sometimes the production costs in those countries cannot be ascertained, and it is difficult to apply the anti-dumping legislation, even difficult to define whether dumping has taken place.

The powers given the government under this bill have to be used sparingly, not as a form of national protective policy or as a way of getting around agreements that we have entered into under GATT. This is very important. But on occasion some of our major industries that are large employers of labour are seriously jeopardized, and I can foresee the necessity for the government to take immediate action. When such an occasion arises is not the time to start thinking about legislation. The legislation should be in existence and ready for implementation. Therefore we would like to see such blanket powers included in this bill.

There have been occasions when the provisions of the act have been inadequate to protect the national interest. A year or two ago minerals like copper and nickel were in short supply and Canada, one of the major producers of these commodities, faced shortages of these minerals for its own industries. Our own industries were not able to obtain the copper and nickel which they needed, while many exportations were taking place. During that period the Minister of Trade and Commerce was asked concerning his intentions to act in this regard. The answer we received was that exports are more important than looking after the internal needs of our own industries. This to me is a very unacceptable proposition. If we are to move away from the exportation of raw materials as has been the case in the past and become more of a manufacturing nation, which we are capable of becoming and should become, we must ensure, particularly in those areas where we are major producers of raw materials, that those raw materials are not denied to our own manufacturers. In looking at this bill I do not think such protection is available under the enumerated powers in the bill.
I should also like to say a word about war materials. Under the consolidated Export and Import Permits Act it is clearly indicated that the government of Canada has the power to prohibit the export of war materials of various kinds. Our quarrel is simply that the powers possessed under this act have not been exercised in order to carry out what I believe is the considered judgment of the Canadian people. We have been guilty of complicity in the war in Viet Nam by sending war materials from this country to the United States. Our people did not want to participate i a that war and yet our government has

Therefore there are two points which our party wishes to emphasize. First, the bill should be enlarged to include the emergency powers that may be necessary to protect industries which are in danger of extinction in this country, especially those industries which we have made a decision to support. Second, the government should pay more attention to the desire of the Canadian people in respect of controlling our own future, our utilization of our resources and our unwillingness to participate in other people's immoral wars. Mr. Speaker, similar to the two preceding speakers I should like to say that the Export and Import Permits Act and the amendments now before us should be used effectively under the changing conditions in Canada generally. In the field of agriculture particularly we have a tremendous ability to produce. There is also a tremendous ability to produce on the part of our neighbour to the south and the European communities. It was stated by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson), as reported in the press, that there is scarcely a developed nation in the western world that is not capable of producing a great deal more agricultural products than can be consumed by that nation. I assume that is the reason the dairy commission is specifically included in this bill.
In respect of the production of feed grain in western Canada and corn in Ontario we find that the market is flooded with these products from other countries and that our own producers are at a serious disadvantage. I do not think we should allow ourselves to drift-I repeat, drift-into the position where we will be buying supplies from overseas or from our neighbour to the south which we can produce efficiently and easily at home. If we do not follow the policy of using our own resources we will find ourselves trying to get foreign exchange to pay for products which we should be producing here. As has been mentioned, this applies to turkeys and rape-seed in western Canada and to vegetable production as well.

I hope the government will use the power it is taking through this bill. In the agricultural sector particularly I believe we are entering what might be described as a selective position. Mr. Speaker, I want to say that the removal of the $5,000 limit in respect of which the minister's approval is required for construction of any facility on a navigable water makes every dock, boathouse, launching ramp or other facility on a navigable water subject to approval by the federal Minister of Transport. In addition, facilities already in existence can now be ordered removed. The act, as this bill proposes to amend it, will apply to every work which projects over a body of water, no matter how small. It will include even a couple of planks built on a couple of posts on a very small stream in any part of Canada.
This is one of the most dangerous pieces of legislation ever brought before parliament. I
5332	COMMONS
Navigable Waters Protection Act am positive that the Department of Transport could not possibly enforce it. At the present time there are in existence many facilities such as boathouses, wharves, launching ramps and marinas which have not been approved by the minister. If the owner could prove that these facilities cost less than $5,000, before these amendments are adopted, he would be fairly safe to go ahead without applying to the departments. These amendments remove that $5,000 limit. Every navigational facility will now be brought under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. Facilities of any size on any body of water no matter how small will be covered by this measure.
The interpretation of the word "navigable" has never been made clear, and I appreciate the difficulties involved. At the moment there are two obvious tests. There is a difference in the interpretation of "navigable" by the Department of Public Works and the interpretation by the Department of Transport. The term "navigable water" was interpreted by a number of witnesses who appeared before the transport committee as any body of water on which you can paddle a canoe. Therefore this measure has been extended to every situation involving a body of water in Canada.
I have been very close to the work done by the harbours and rivers branch of the Department of Public Works because I represent a part of the country in which there are many cottagers and tourist operators. Whenever they go to the Department of Public Works seeking approval for the construction of a wharf, a launching ramp or a boathouse on a small body of water, they have been told that this was never the intention of the B.N.A. Act in respect of navigable waters. These people have been told that the B.N.A. Act was never intended to cover small structures such as launching ramps or boathouses on small lakes or rivers. They have been informed that the B.N.A. Act was intended to relate to large navigable waters such as the oceans, the Great Lakes and larger inland lakes. They have been told not to ask the government to build a dock on Beaver Creek, for example, because that is not a navigable water in terms of this act.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
We now have the Department of Transport coming along and saying that this is all right for the Department of Public Works but the Department of Transport will control navigation on any body of water no matter what its size. This has been a real problem and it has
[Mr. Aiken.1

not been cleared up. In fact, the amendments to the Navigable Waters Protection Act that we are now considering make the situation worse. Just a week ago I was at a meeting in connection with the facilities in Algonquin Park. One outfitter there was disgusted that a body of water in the park in which he was interested had been declared navigable. He said there were six month old frogs in that creek that had not even learned to swim; yet it had been declared a navigable water.
This is a very sloppy piece of legislation and the Department of Transport cannot possibly carry out its provisions. They cannot possibly carry out their responsibilities because the act will provide that every person who proposes to build a dock, launching ramp or boathouse which extends over the water will be required to obtain a permit from the Department of Transport. If he does not do so, he runs the risk of the department coming along later and saying: We are sorry, but you must take this construction down. People who propose to build these structures will not have the protection that exists now under the section which provides that if the structure costs under $5,000 they are safe. Now there is no limitation. This means that under the legislation the department will undertake to receive applications from anybody in Canada who wants to build a dock or a boathouse. I know the department cannot do it; it is an impossible task.
A few years ago the province of Ontario tried to catch up on their responsibility in this matter and found it was impossible. There were docks and boathouses all over the province and they could not possibly do it. That is only one province. I do not know how the Department of Transport expects to carry out its responsibilities in this regard for the whole of Canada. This will be a carte blanche for every federal marine agent to go to a private owner in Canada and say: Remove your boathouse because you did not obtain a permit. They will be able to do this without any reason being expressed.
This legislation will also make it possible for a cottager to go to the Department of Transport and say that the fellow next door to him is building a dock and he wants the department to stop it. He can ask whether his neighbour has obtained a permit to build the dock. If the department says it did not bother to require a permit to be obtained because it was just a small dock, the man making the complaint can have the building of the dock stopped because his neighbour does not have a permit. If this man is not stopped, the

department is derelict in its duty. If he is stopped, it is unfair to the man who is trying to do exactly what his neighbour has done. I am seriously concerned about this situation.
The minister tried to clear this matter up at the report stage. I do not have his exact words, but in essence he said that the department was not going to worry about little docks with a couple of planks. This was also said in the committee. But it is not what the bill says. The bill says that included within its provisions is every little dock with a couple of planks. I ask, Mr. Speaker: At what point is the Department of Transport going to carry out its responsibility? At what point is it going to be derelict in its duty? I think this legislation leaves the situation wide open.
I should like to mention the situation in which the provincial authorities are placed. At the present time, if you want to build a boathouse or a dock and want to be sure it will not be torn down, you must go to the provincial department of lands and forests, or whatever department is concerned, and obtain a permit to occupy the land under the water because it is provincial crown land. Therefore you must either obtain a patent of ownership for that little piece of crown land under the water, or an annual permit to occupy it, that is, a licence of occupation.
This situation has created a mess for the province because all the docks built without permits are there and a lot more are being built without permits. Some are being built with permits. It is an impossible situation because there are in Canada hundreds of thousands of facilities of this type. It is impossible for even the provincial authorities to regulate this matter. I remember that about 15 or 20 years ago the provincial government of Ontario decided to survey the situation with regard to its responsibility for docks and boathouses on inland lakes. After they looked at the situation for a while they decided it was an impossible task and had to leave it alone. Now we have the federal department wanting to take on the same responsibility in connection with ten provinces and the territories, despite the fact that to my knowledge it is a job that no provincial authority has been able to handle.
If at the present time you want to build a dock with two planks and a couple of posts, you must go to the provincial authority and obtain a licence to occupy the land under the water. Now you will also have to go to the federal Department of Transport and obtain a licence to build a facility on the surface of

There is nothing in this bill that says how far such a construction shall project before it obstructs navigation. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few comments on Bill S-19 to amend the Navigable Waters Protection Act. While the bill before us does bring in some good changes, I felt that the over-all act is still wholly inadequate. In the committee and in the house the bill was discussed and I hoped that one or two major amendments would be brought forward by members on the government side.
I do not know if all members of the house are aware of the fact that the Navigable Waters Protection Act does not apply to all organizations in Canada. For example, the main users of our water resources are provincial and federal Crown corporations. They are the ones that use the navigable waters of this nation, and we find that they are not covered by this act. I think they should be. In my frank opinion the government and the minister are derelict in their duty to the people of Canada when they fail to include the main users of our great water resources. It is a disgraceful attitude for the government in the year 1969 to ignore the damage which can be done to water resources by failing to bringing in another amendment to include Crown corporations under the act.
This afternoon I would like to speak rather briefly to point out why I feel further amendments should have been made to Bill S-19. I am very disturbed by the fact that Crown corporations are excluded from the provisions of the Act. I come from the province of British Columbia where we have had some pretty sad experiences of what can happen to the navigable waters of a province merely because there was no agency that could insist on a proper job being done when certain hydro dams, for example, were being built. Here we have a bill amending the Navigable Waters Protection Act and excluding those agencies which most often do not take into consideration all the effects of the damming of certain rivers or lakes. This is the reason I suggest to the government that the bill is anything but adequate.
I feel that Canadians are very anxious that we exercise much tighter control over the use of our water resources than we have had in the past. During the committee hearing the legal counsel pointed out to the members of the committee that unless we specifically include in the act provincial and federal Crown corporations they will be exempted because of a clause in the Interpretation Act.
It seems to me that the greatest omission that has been made is that these Crown corporations are not going to be forced to do the will

DEBATES	February 10, 1969
of the federal government. Farther on in the act under section 12 we find that the federal government may exempt any group, individual or corporation from the provisions of the act if it so desires. If they can provide a good case for the construction of a dam or the flooding of a certain area or the diversion of a river, then the federal government has the right, under the act as it now stands, to exempt them from the provisions of the act. But if Crown corporations are not included- and they are not included either in this bill or in the old act-then they are home free and can do anything they wish in so far as the damming of waterways is concerned.
I would like to give the house several good examples of what has happened because we have not had sufficient protection in the act to insist on surveys being made before projects were commenced. It seems to me essential in this day and age that in the exploitation of our water resources we consider every aspect before proceeding with a project. If dams are to be built, I feel that proper ecological surveys should be made. We should know the results upon the local economy, upon wild life, vegetation, pollution, fish, tourism and a number of other related aspects. I hope that the concept of the multiple use of our resources will replace the blind, single-purpose development which apparently we have in Canada today.
I also want to point out that when the Navigable Waters Protection Act was before the house for second reading the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) spoke about the damaging effects which the Portage Mountain Dam in British Columbia was having on the whole of the Mackenzie River system. He pointed out that the provincial government did not go to the federal government for permission to build the dam. Protests were made but nothing was done. I think this is an excellent example of the need for control. Absolutely no ecological studies were made. As a result, we find that a neighbouring province, Alberta, and the area to the north of that province, are suffering. I am certain something could have been worked out to the satisfaction of all the governments concerned had full and proper surveys been undertaken before the project commenced. No improvement will be possible until an amendment along the lines of the one I have suggested has been enacted.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
About a week ago I received a letter from a group of interested university people on the
February 10, 1989	COMMONS
very subject upon which I am speaking. It outlined clearly the need for immediate action in the field of resource control and should be of interest to every member of the house. I understand the letter has been sent to several newspapers; if any hon. member would like a copy of it I would be glad to supply one. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read it into the record. I could outline the gist of it, but I think reading it would give a clearer picture of what these people are asking us to do. The letter comes from the Department of Electrical Engineering of the University of Alberta, Edmonton. It is dated January 28, 1969, and was addressed in this case to myself, though, as I say, it was sent to several newspapers. It reads as follows:
We are concerned that there seems to be a lack of policy by both the federal and provincial governments in Canada with regard to evaluating the ecological implications of the development of our natural resources. It appears that in the exploitation of these resources little or no attention is being given to the consequences upon the local economy, wildlife, vegetation, prevention of lake and river pollution, preservation of scenic beauty and other related values which ultimately mean so much to the Canadian people.
For example, it has recently been brought to our attention that there has been a considerable disruption of the ecology in the Peace River delta area in northeastern Alberta. A large portion of this area lies in Wood Buffalo National Park. Before the Portage Mountain Dam was built, the spring floodcrest on the Peace River provided a natural damming of the waters of the Athabasca River. This damming of the Athabasca River permitted it to back up and flood the forementioned delta area. This annual flooding was a vital factor in the ecology of the region. As a result, the area was able to support large numbers of muskrat, and to provide good spawning conditions for whitefish and goldeye in Lake Athabasca and adjacent waters. The muskrat provided a livelihood for the local Indian population-approximately 1,200 people-and the fish have supported commercial fishing for many years.
Now, all this has been threatened by the Portage Mountain Dam which will eliminate the floodcrest on the Peace River. Already, the water level of Lake Athabasca is some eight feet below normal, and is threatening the whitefish population. Both Richardson Lake and Mamawi Lake are dry and Lake Claire is now only five feet deep and is expected to freeze solid this winter. It has been estimated that in this year alone a quarter of a million muskrat will perish due to abnormally low water levels. The lack of water in Mamawi Lake has virtually eliminated the goldeye run in Birch River.
The above ecological changes were predicted and brought to the attention of the provincial authorities while the Portage Mountain Dam was in its planning stages. Apparently the information went unheeded.
Once more a dam is being planned without any apparent attention being given to the ecological
DEBATES	5335
Navigable Waters Protection Act repercussions. We are referring to the proposed Bighorn Dam on the North Saskatchewan River near Nordegg, Alberta. Already it is apparent that this dam will considerably affect the local wildlife population and at this stage one can only guess as to what else. Since we are very concerned about the possible consequences of this project, we are bringing it to your attention in the hope that you can initiate a critical review of this problem. We hope that a proper review of all aspects of the Bighorn Dam will serve as a precedent for similar future projects.
We are continuing to investigate this matter and will forward to you any additional information.
This letter is signed by seven professors from the department, and if hon. members wish their names I shall gladly read them. It underlines the very point I am making. We are allowing projects of this sort to take place in the absence of any surveys to find out what the over-all picture is likely to be in a few years time. It is simple enough. Engineers in our hydro corporations, for example, are given a job to do. They are asked to check as to the possibility of damming a river. They do this, and I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, they do a good job. Next, they turn in an engineering report stating how much the dam will cost, the amount of power it will supply, and so on. They are trained to do this. But they do not take into consideration the various points to which clear reference is made in the letter I have just read.
I say that as Members of Parliament for the Dominion of Canada it is our duty to see that we get the best possible return from the use of our resources-in this particular case, the water resources of the nation. You know, Mr. Speaker, that we have some excellent examples to the contrary in British Columbia; I have mentioned some of them in debate previously. I think it is the utmost stupidity on the part of the federal and provincial government to close their eyes to the need for proper reports being made before taking steps which might allow our resources to get away from us. In British Columbia we have a number of fine hydro projects, but in most instances they were designed and built for one purpose only. The ecological effects behind the dams on the areas affected were never taken into consideration.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
In every province of Canada lakes have been flooded without the land first being cleared. I agree that it is necessary for us in this country to have cheap electric power. We build dams in order that cheap power may be supplied to our people. But included in the development costs of any power project must
5336	COMMONS
Navigable Waters Protection Act be the cost of studies undertaken to determine the effects on wildlife in the area to be flooded. Ecological factors have been ignored. That is why I suggest that Crown corporations ought to be brought under this legislation. We could ask Crown corporations to lay before us alternatives to projects to be undertaken. Crown corporations would examine the general ecology of an area to be flooded and determine how much it would cost to replace wildlife which might be destroyed.
I can tell you, sir, what has happened in British Columbia. I have spoken both inside and outside this chamber on a number of occasions on what has been happening in British Columbia. We built the High Arrow Dam; yet no ecological studies of the Arrow Lakes, which stretch for 140 miles, were made before building the dam, the result being that between 69 and 90 per cent of the area in which fish spawn has been destroyed.

speechtext: That is a provincial matter.

speechtext:
Yes, it may be a provincial matter but navigable waters come under the jurisdiction of the federal government. If Crown corporations were included we might have some planning and prevent losses of spawning grounds. Questions should be asked. How are the destroyed fish to be replaced? Are you going to build fish hatcheries, or ladders up falls so that fish can climb farther up mountain streams to spawn? Will fish different from those which have been destroyed be introduced into the new lakes with the hope they will spawn? Such questions ought to have been answered by studies.
A few miles south of the Canadian border and close to the town of Creston the United States authorities last year began to build the Libby Dam. The reservoir basin behind the lake will spill 40 miles into Canada. Yet two or three years before the United States authorities began building the dam they ordered an ecological survey of the affected area. They wanted to know what would happen when the area was flooded. I have a report of those studies in my files. The United States authorities knew exactly what had to be done to replace lost spawning grounds and to preserve wildlife. Alternative plans were laid out. We in Canada should expect nothing less from our Crown corporations. Those who benefit from hydroelectric developments ought to insist on such studies.
As we obtain more and more leisure time our people will look to the great outdoors for recreation. The legislators of this nation ought

DEBATES	February 10, 1969
to make sure that our natural resources are passed on to future generations unimpaired. We must not destroy what we have.
In British Columbia a dam is being built on the Columbia River at Mica Creek. They are blocking off a lake 125 miles long; yet the provincial government will not clear all the standing timber from the area. Oh, a small chunk will be cleared so that from the top of the reservoir you will think that a beautiful job has been done. But for centuries that reservoir will be polluted because drifting, rotten trees will spoil the water, and what should be a recreational area and a navigable water system will be ruined. You can see the same sort of thing in Duncan Lake, also known as Bennett's Lake. It is partly in my riding. The condition of that lake is a national disgrace. Most of the land was not cleared before flooding and you can hardly get a rowboat through the upper portion of it because of all the drifting material in the water. Here in this parliament we talk about conserving resources for our people and yet we allow this sort of thing to take place. Here we have a chance to bring Crown corporations under the Navigable Waters Protection Act and prevent such pollution. Even if the federal government must pay for studies to be undertaken, it ought to do so. We ought to preserve our resources and not allow their stupid destruction, as has taken place in scattered areas from the east to the west coasts of Canada.
Accordingly I move, seconded by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg):
That Bill S-19 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications for the purpose of reconsidering Clause 4 thereof.
The purpose of reconsidering clause 4 is to allow us to bring federal and provincial Crown corporations under the act.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to second the amendment moved by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding). I am sure that in the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) was made aware of our discontent that Crown corporations were not included under the provisions of this bill. I am also aware that he may try to substantiate his case by referring to the fact that this would involve a constitutional issue. I respectfully suggest that this matter could be resolved at a later time and the Crown corporations should be included under the provisions of the bill because so far as the constitutional issue is concerned I believe the minister is trying to muddy the waters. I suggest that quite an amount of water could be muddied if the bill is allowed to pass in its present form.
I know that my colleagues from Winnipeg North Centre and Winnipeg North are aware of the situation in Manitoba, and no doubt the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orli-kow) will speak about it. A real storm has blown up in regard to the action of a Crown corporation in taking it upon itself to construct a dam which adversely affected navigable waters in that province and below the

province. The question has been asked in one press article:
What happens when a Crown corporation floods out a community of nearly 600 Indians and Metis in the name of industrial progress?
This could be used as an analogy in any province of Canada. If we allow situations like this to exist and do nothing about them the House of Commons will be held suspect in the eyes of the people adversely affected.
Various articles have appeared in the press about this situation and I shall refer briefly to a number of them. One of them stated:
Five university professors presented a brief to the government which cast a wholly different light on the situation. Conservationists, wildlife experts, engineers, ecologists, more professors of various disciplines, and other knowledgeable people began to issue statements.
It is ridiculous that a province should be allowed to implement a program of its own without sending its engineering studies to the federal government so that there may be more than one party involved in the preparation and the planning, particularly when more than one province may be adversely affected. I quote again:
The report, prepared by the provincial resources department's own experts, documented that Hydro's plan would result in "devastation" to an area equal to 20 per cent of the province's total territory. Its authors warned that about 2,175 square miles of now beautiful lakes, rivers and potential resort areas would be rendered sterile; that all wildlife habitat, and revenue derived from wildlife, would be lost from the area for at least 100 years and that the seaport of Churchill would suffer serious repercussions-
With respect to that one point alone, the adverse effect on the port of Churchill which it is suggested could result from this plan, I believe hon. members would agree that this bill should be sent back to committee for further consideration.
It was also pointed out that various types of wildlife in the area would be affected. It was stated that flooding in the area can bring about a radical change in a huge Canada goose nesting ground. It was also pointed out that the project will eliminate a great chunk of barren ground caribou wintering range in Manitoba.
I could point out many other arguments to prove that the province itself should not have the prime and prior right to construct a dam on any river which would impair the navigable portions of the river. I had thought that the Minister without Portfolio would have an answer prepared in time for the third reading of this bill, but that has not been the case.
February 10, 1969	COMMONS
We got no answer from the minister and so naturally my colleague from Kootenay West had to present this amendment.
Many experts have pointed out the problems to the provincial authorities, with the result that they are taking a second look to see whether or not the dam in question should be constructed and the water diverted. Even though construction of the dam has started, and it would not be economical to continue the project without ensuring the provision of the added water facilities, we must look at the social consequences to affected communities. In this area I suggest that the federal government has a prime responsibility along with the province to make sure that the matter is looked at in its entirety.
I should like to refer to a brief presented by Professor Edward Kuiper, former chief engineer in the provincial water resources branch and a consultant to Manitoba Hydro in that capacity. He said that no alternatives to the proposed Southern Indian Lake diversion scheme were ever adequately studied by Manitoba Hydro. I suggest that this is a clear indication that such schemes should be studied in their entirety to determine what effect they will have on the communities involved. This was not done in Manitoba. Professor Kuiper's brief added:
Therefore no one is presently in a position to state that the proposed high-level Southern Indian Lake diversion is better or worse than any of the four alternative diversions.
Again this points up the fact that there should have been further discussions and consultations before any decision was rendered in this case. The people in that area have been very adversely affected. I suggest that the federal government should consider amendments to this legislation whereby such matters will be covered. I am positive that if the federal government does not assume this responsibility the provinces will not assume it either. They are primarily concerned with their own economies because they must consider the long-range economic effects without taking into account all the social consequences.
I heartily support the amendment that has been proposed. Many things can be accomplished in this house if the government is willing to tackle them. In this case I say the government must have the will, and this house as a whole must ensure that this legislation properly protects all those who are adversely affected.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to support the amendment moved by my colleague from Kootenay West. I specifically do so because of the tremendous problems raised by the plan of Manitoba Hydro, acting for the Manitoba government, to divert the waters of the Nelson River in order to construct a very large hydro project. This government and this parliament are involved and ought to be very concerned about this project because the former government approved the expenditure by the people of Canada of a very large amount of money to help pay for this project.
I have no objection to the development of the Nelson River. This is a tremendously important project that will produce a very large amount of power which can be used by the people of Manitoba and may indeed be sold to the province of Ontario or the province of Saskatchewan. It is expected that the surplus will be sold in the middle west of the United States. However, it is disturbing to say the least that a project of this tremendous scope, which will involve a billion or more dollars, is being proceeded with while the facts about it, if they are known, are known only to the government of Manitoba.
In the past four or five years the government of Manitoba commissioned a number of studies by various expert groups to determine the facts involved in the project. A key part of the whole plan is the diversion of the waters of the Churchill River into the Nelson River in order to provide a more regular flow in the Nelson River where power plants will be constructed. It is quite evident from reports which the newspapers in Winnipeg have been able to obtain that not all the facts in respect of the transfer of water from the one river to the other have been taken into account.
My colleague, the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Skoberg), has referred to the effect on the Indians at Southern Indian Lake. This community of 600 Indian and Metis people is probably the only community of its kind in Manitoba, if not in all Canada, where not a single person receives welfare from either the federal or provincial governments and where the breadwinners earn from $3,000 to $6,000 or $8,000 a year. For an Indian or a Metis this is a fantastic income. These 600 people are being told by the hydro authorities that they must move because their community will be under 35 feet of water.
February 10, 1969

Navigable Waters Protection Act
It is true that hydro has offered them alternative sites, but a group of university professors hired by the government of Manitoba has questioned, because of the way in which the area is to be flooded, whether in fact there will remain a viable fishing industry. All these factors were studied by the government or by Manitoba Hydro. Even though public hearings have been held and even though the Indians have hired eminent counsel, to date the government of Manitoba and Manitoba Hydro have categorically refused to make public the studies that were made. If there has even been a better illustration of a kangaroo court I do not know where you would find it because the government, which permitted hearings by its water conservation board into the effects of the project, refuses to give to the Indians or others concerned the documents which it commissioned. It well may be that the government would argue that there are differences of opinion between the experts, but surely it ought not to be the right of any agency, whether federal, provincial or private, to say that although they have the information and all the reports they will decide what they will make public. Surely that type of thing should be ruled out from the start.
As I say, we have an important role to play here because, first, the federal government is providing a substantial part of the money for the Nelson River project and, second, the federal government is the trustee for the Indians. We have always said that the restrictions on Indians by virtue of the Indian Act exist because the Indians are not ready to look after themselves and are not sufficiently well educated or adjusted to live in our modern wage-earning, profit-making society. We say that we, the great white fathers, must protect the Indians from themselves. I notice that the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand) is listening. This is the attitude we have taken. I submit that we cannot have it both ways. We cannot take the position taken almost every day by the Indian Affairs Branch that we will decide what is best for the Indians and then take no action when a group of 600 Indians are to be moved forcibly and against their will from the community in which they have lived for many years.
I shall come back to the Indians in a moment, but I wish to make clear that it is not only the Indians affected in respect of whom we have a responsibility. When I was in Winnipeg I was told that if this project goes ahead and if the waters of the Churchill River are diverted into the Nelson River, it

is quite likely that the flow of the Churchill River will be cut by as much as 75 per cent. If that happens there will immediately be an effect on the port of Churchill. The minister as a member from Saskatchewan, should have a vital interest in the port of Churchill. Churchill has been having difficulties because of the short season and poor town planning. If 75 per cent of the water of the Churchill River is diverted there will be times of the year at Churchill when there will not be sufficient water to meet the drinking and sanitation needs of the town.
One might ask what the situation will be if the salt water from Hudson Bay should flow up the Churchill River. I do not know and I do not know whether the minister is informed in this regard. It is stated in one of the reports which the government of Manitoba has refused to make public that if the water is diverted the flow of the Thompson River as it passes through the town of Thompson would certainly be very much greater than it would normally be. It is hoped that in ten years time Thompson will be the size of Sudbury. We are told that the Thompson River will rise 20 or more feet, that bridges will have to be rebuilt and that the whole area will be changed. What will happen as a result?
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
Certainly the federal government has a responsibility and ought to look into this whole situation. Unless the amendment moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Kootenay West, is accepted, we will have no opportunity to do the kind of thing we are suggesting the federal government ought to do. Before a navigable stream is allowed to be changed as a result of the plans of any agency we should make sure that all the information required is made public. This should be done whether a federal or provincial agency is involved. It should also be done even when a private agency proposes the change.
We talk very frequently about our desire that the Indians should learn to speak for themselves so they do not need a white member of the government or the bureaucracy, a social worker, a do-gooder or a magistrate to speak for them. The Indians of Manitoba have taken us at our word. They have probably gone farther than any other group of Indians in the country in creating an organization to speak for them. They are doing so in an increasingly effective manner. I should like to put on record what the president of the Manitoba Indian Brotherhood has said. I
February 10, 1969
quote what Chief David Courchene said, as reported in an article in the Winnipeg Free Press of January 22, 1969:
The Manitoba Indian Brotherhood president, David Courchene said in a statement Tuesday the brotherhood is "appalled with the arbitrary action taken by the government".
He went on to state:
-the procedure showed the government's lack of concern for Indian people.
"Such action in the midst of negotiations is a clear and obvious indication of the government's lack of consideration of Indian people. It is also an obvious indication of a lack of good faith for, while inviting participation at hearings .. . decisions have already been made.
The government obviously subscribes to the 'might is right' philosophy in negotiation. We are sure the people of Manitoba will be as incensed, shocked and appalled at the Manitoba government's denial of basic justice and lack of good faith."
The people of Manitoba are appalled and they expect that the federal government, which as a vital stake in this whole question, will not hide behind what I consider to be the spurious argument that an agreement has been reached and there is nothing it can do about it, or the argument that the Indians are not members of a reserve and therefore are not the responsibility of the federal government.
I hope the government will not hide behind the argument that at this late stage it cannot amend this measure in the way the hon. member for Kootenay West has suggested. I appeal to the government to accept this very moderate and sensible amendment in order that it may have the time and the opportunity to undo what I consider to be a basic injustice to the people of northern Manitoba, be they Indian or white.

The second of the major areas in which I feel that our slowness in law reform has worked prejudice for the individual has been that of the civil law under federal jurisdiction. Here again I should like to pick two examples: The priority over other creditors which the Crown claims for taxes; and, the heavy stick which Crown expropriators swing against small property owners. In respect of the first, a brief review of the federal taxing statutes illustrates what an advantage the treasury claims over other creditors. With regard to income tax and sales tax, for example, the respective laws provide that all taxes, penalties and costs can be claimed by the Crown as a debt due in either the Exchequer Court or other competent court.
In the case of income tax-
It was my unhappy experience with one of my clients that the income tax people moved in. The hon. member here refers to their moving in as a group of in-laws and hastens to add, quite unlike his own in-laws.
In the case of income tax, what the Department of National Revenue commonly does is to issue a certificate that the tax has not been paid. That certificate simply is registered in the court as proof that there is a sum due. It is entirely equivalent to the situation of a businessman who has sued and obtained a judgment for a debt. The difference is that the Crown is given the right to skip the ordinary court proceedings and has the amount of the debt set at what it claims, not at what a court has found. This situation works a particular hardship on other businesses in the case of the bankruptcy of a debtor business-
In another situation, the priority given for government taxes works a particular hardship in the case of the intrepid creditor pursuing the hidden assets of a chronic non-payer. The writ of extent, which is the authority issued by the Exchequer Court to collect the tax debt against property, can be used by the department to claim prior security in hidden assets smoked out by an energetic creditor. The creditor does all the work and the revenuers move in to reap the benefit-

Surely the important principle here in connection with bankruptcy or non-payment of debts is who can best afford to bear the loss, the small businessman or the vast resources of the government? The Minister without Portfolio from Manitoba (Mr. Richardson) who was piloting the legislation through the committee, left the impression that he looked upon the proposed amendment as a very serious one. Were it not for the ruling of the committee chairman the minister would have sought advice from committee members on the amendment, which at that time was moved by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding), the mover of the amendment now before the house. The difficulty was procedural and arose from the fact that the hon. member either was not present in committee during discussion of clause 4 or had omitted to move his amendment to clause 4. There was an understanding in the committee, however, that we would be returning to clause 1 for a general discussion. At the conclusion of the general discussion on clause 1 the hon. member for Kootenay West endeavoured to move the amendment he has placed before the house today. At that time the Minister without Portfolio from Manitoba said, as reported at page 219 of Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence No. 12 of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
If it is to be left to me to decide, then I would appreciate the opportunity to have further views of the Committee. I think that we have a very serious difficulty here, as I explained when we talked about this matter last week. It was considered before the amendments were suggested and brought forward for consideration.

He goes on to say:
Can we have your permission to discuss this? I may be out of order here in the face of your ruling-
Then he was interrupted by the committee chairman who ruled that he could not entertain an amendment to clause 4 since clause 4 had already been adopted by the committee. Yet, it was understood by most of us that we were having a general discussion on clause 1.
Later, when replying to a question raised by a committee member when we were discussing procedure and wondering whether we could consider the amendment in committee, the minister said, as reported at page 221 of the evidence of the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications for January 27:
Yes. On this point of jurisdiction, yes. This is why I said that I do not know the full feelings of the Committee but I think I am beginning to sense them now. Certainly it will be given every possible consideration.
Then clause 1 was agreed to and the bill was passed in committee. The minister gave an undertaking to the committee, as will be found if one reads page 221 of the evidence. I understood that the minister was taking the matter under advisement and would report to his colleagues in cabinet what he felt were the views of the committee. In that basis, even though the amendment had not been adopted, we allowed the bill to pass the committee stage.
Today the hon. member for Kootenay West has moved a similar amendment and I would be interested to hear the remarks of the Minister without Portfolio from Manitoba, who had the responsibility of piloting this bill through committee. I am sure that his colleague, the Minister without Portfolio from Saskatchewan (Mr. Lang) will be pleased that he does not have the responsibility of answering hon. members' questions. That hon. gentleman has had the responsibility all day of piloting the various stages of bills through the house.
During his speech the hon. member for Kootenay West, the mover of the amendment, said there were serious deficiencies in the legislation which he would endeavour to correct with his amendment. He said that the bill endeavours to regulate and to impose penalties; it regulates what individuals may or may not do in erecting works or obstructions to navigation. He also said, I believe, that the provisions of the bill in their present form would not apply to federal or provincial
Navigable Waters Protection Act Crown corporations set up to develop hydroelectric power. These developments have taken place in British Columbia. Indeed, he said that similar problems exist in every province of this country. Most provinces of Canada have provincial Crown corporations set up to develop hydro-electric power. These developments have led to certain works being done near navigable waters. For instance, many rivers have been diverted in the interest of hydroelectric development and as a result navigation of those waters, as defined in this act, has been seriously impeded. Actually, the navigable waters no longer exist.
I submit we should not forget that conservation is important, and this legislation has aspects touching on conservation. It is necessary to protect and conserve our navigable waters.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
We are concerned, too, with conservation in its broader aspect, that of preserving our rivers and streams for present and future generations to enjoy. Conservation is an important subject and we are concerned particularly here with the development of hydroelectric installations by Crown corporations. The hon. member for Kootenay West has referred to projects of this kind in British Columbia. I could refer to developments which are taking place in my own province of Newfoundland, and in Labrador. Many rivers have been diverted for the sake of hydroelectric power generation. Rivers have been dammed, impeding navigation on those rivers in the strictest sense in the process. This is what the bill before us sets out to regulate. Yet, we find this surprising anomaly in the provisions before us, one which the minister himself admitted when he was piloting the measure through the committee.
I think there is only one reasonable way of solving this difficulty. The government should accept this amendment because, after all, all it asks is that the bill be referred back to committee. I would point out that we are dealing here with amending legislation, legislation which cannot be considered as being of an urgent nature. If the bill were referred back to committee, the committee could go into these questions in great detail. Then, the minister could fulfil his undertaking to reach, if possible, a consensus among members of the committee, and proceed along more satisfactory lines. Furthermore, this course would enable the government to study the constitutional aspects involved and possibly to consider having the bill referred to the next
February 10, 1969

Navigable Waters Protection Act meeting of resource ministers. Certainly, the bill in its present form makes no sense to us on this side and I am sure it makes no sense to supporters of the government. And if the remarks of the Minister without Portfolio <Mr. Richardson) are any indication, I contend it makes no sense to him, either.
I would refer hon. members to the minutes and proceedings of the committee on transport and communications for January 27 when this bill was the subject of clause by clause study. If hon. members, and the minister in particular, wish to approach this matter in a reasonable way I suggest they should accept this amendment. By so doing they would show they were really interested in the subject and that the government has confidence in the work of committees of the house under the new Standing Orders. After all, we are not here merely to rubber stamp committee reports or amending legislation. speechtext:
As the house knows, this bill received second reading, was referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, and is now back in this chamber for third reading. It deals with the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. More particularly, it increases the number of commercial lenders and makes a new provision with respect to interest rates, one which is more realistic in present circumstances. Finally the bill increases the liability of the government as a result of the new financial provisions in the proposed amendments to the act.
I should like to refer, now, to another desirable amendment to the act. This proposed amendment was incorporated in a notice
February 10, 1969

Fisheries Improvement Loans Act which I sent to the Clerk of the House on February 5, 1969. I also commended it to the Committee on Fisheries and Forestry during the course of its deliberations on Thursday, February 6, as many hon. members present know. The notice I sent to the Clerk of the House of Commons was to the effect that after Bill C-151 had been reported back to this house I would propose under standing order 75 the following motion:
That Bill C-151, an act to amend the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, be amended by renumbering clause 2 thereof as subclause (2) of clause 2 and by adding as subclause (1) of clause 2 the following:
2.	(1) All that portion of paragraph (d) of
subsection (1) of section 3 of the said Act following subparagraph (ii) thereof is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"did not exceed twenty-five thousand dollars;"
As hon. members know, the intent of this amendment would be to raise the maximum individual fisheries loan limit from $10,000 to $25,000. I understand the authorities were concerned about whether or not this amendment constituted an additional charge on the Consolidated Revenue fund, or, alternatively, an increase in the contingent liability of the government. They were concerned, in other words, lest a message of recommendation of the Governor General might be necessary before such an amendment would be in order. I say "might" because I am personally not convinced that this amendment would, if carried, increase the liability of the government over the $20 million covered by this legislation.
There is, however, another and important reservation. I am advised that the proposed amendment is not acceptable on another and altogether different ground for reasons which are only now becoming clear because they relate to the new rules under which this house is operating. I now find that any amendment of the character to which I alluded in the Committee on Fisheries and Forestry, or such as I have read into the record, would not be acceptable because the intent of the amendment is sufficiently different from the main provisions of Bill C-151 as to disqualify it. Accordingly, at least in the opinion of the authorities, it cannot be contemplated at any stage after the adoption of the motion for second reading.
I, personally, believe that the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act must be amended in the way suggested, in other words, so as to permit the maximum amount of a loan to be

increased from $10,000 to $25,000. I am therefore proposing, with the support of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald), to introduce another bill which will contain a single clause to this effect. It will be identical in almost every respect with the bill to amend the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act which was passed in 1965, dealing exclusively with the ceiling on individual loans.
This is an important provision. I believe it must be enacted, and enacted soon. I find that fishermen across the country need loans in excess of $10,000. Indeed, it is debatable whether $25,000 is adequate for their purposes, either for building new boats or for re-equipping existing vessels. I, therefore, undertake to bring in a new bill and, as I have said, I have the assurance of the office of the President of the Privy Council that this will receive top priority. That is my statement, Mr. Speaker.
