speechtext:
I listened with interest, Mr. Speaker, to the statements made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis), and I wish to comment briefly on the bill which is presently before the house.
When the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act received Royal Assent on July 11, 1955, the amount of any loan which could be made to an individual fisherman could not exceed $4,000 and under the terms of the loan it was repayable in full over a period of not more than eight years.
The Act was amended on March 20, 1959 to provide broader coverage to individual fishermen, and the term "fisherman" was more clearly defined. The Act was again amended on March 23, 1962, extending the powers granted to the Minister to June, 1965. On June 23, 1965, the legislation was further revised raising the amount of any loan to fishermen from $4,000 to $10,000, and the repayment period was extended from eight years to ten years.
Since the latter change was made we have seen a substantial rise in the cost of living. Inflation has eroded the purchasing power of the dollar and the cost of goods and services to Canadians has been rising constantly. In my opinion, the act has never been fully utilized by our fishermen; only 2,586 loans to a total of $6,168,800 have been made since it was first brought in as long ago as December, 1955. If the present ceiling is retained, the legislation might well be used to even less effect in the future.
February 10, 1969

It was for this reason I proposed in the committee that the act be amended with specific reference to the amount which might be borrowed and the term set for repayment. I realized that my proposed amendment dealt with the finances of the country. At the same time, the changes I suggested had to do only with loans being made by lending institutions, and since such loans are fully secured, normally by way of mortgages on articles purchased, or liens on the equipment and stock of borrowers, I considered they would not impose any new responsibilities on the government. However, in any event, my amendment was not accepted by the committee.
What do we see happening now with regard to this legislation? There is no proposal to extend the period during which loans have to be repaid. Instead, we are being asked to sign a blank cheque in respect of the rate of interest to be paid by fishermen on loans approved in the future. This represents a vital departure from the provisions of the original act which stated simply that the rate of interest to be charged on the loans was not to exceed 5 per cent per annum, simple interest. We are told, now, that in connection with future loans made under the act fishermen will have to pay a rate of interest to be prescribed by the Governor in Council. That is what the bill says. The rate of interest that is set may well be the same as the rate prescribed under the National Housing Act; or it could be higher. No one knows, except members of the cabinet who will set this rate under order in council. The bill provides, for the guidance of fishermen, that the rate of interest on fishery improvement loans shall be set by the Governor in Council. But this is not what the minister says, Mr. Speaker. He, of course, is privy to discussions in cabinet and he knows what the cabinet proposes to do. Surprisingly, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) has not seen fit so far to amend this legislation in accordance with his statement at the annual meeting of the United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union at Vancouver on Saturday, February 1. This is what the minister had to say about interest rates to the fishermen of British Columbia:

You will be able, within the next month or two, to borrow this money from a wide range of commercial sources at a lower interest rate than the rate paid by the biggest corporation in the country. In a month or two you will be able to borrow money at 71%. This is less than the 8 to 81% which B.C. Packers has to pay for new money.
Fisheries Improvement Loans Act It is only 1% more than the "cost of money" to the Federal Government itself-to the Government of Canada which will be guaranteeing every loan made under our new federal Fisheries Improvement Loans Act.
The interest rate itself is geared to the interest rate paid by the Government of Canada on its long term loans. If Ottawa pays 6% on its new borrowings, then you will be asked to pay 7%. If the federal borrowing rate falls to 5%, then you will pay 6%. If it goes down to 4% then you will pay 5%. The difference is always 1% and the rate under these new loans will go up and down along with the changing cost of money to the Canadian Government in Ottawa.
However, we tried to amend the act; at least, we tried to incorporate the minister's words into the bill. We suggested in the committee that the bill should be amended and that the rate of interest to be charged should be 1 per cent only above what it costs the government to borrow money. We did not receive any support on our effort to have the words of the minister's statement included in the bill. Liberal party supporters seemed more interested in supporting a partisan approach to this matter rather than permitting the official opposition to amend the legislation in keeping with the stated intent of the minister. If it is the government's intention to gear the interest rate on fishery improvement loans to the interest rate paid by the government of Canada on its long term loans, why does it not come out and say so, and spell it out in this legislation? What have you over there to hide from the Canadian fisherman? No wonder the fishermen of Canada to date have looked with obvious mistrust and misgiving at this particular act.
Since the inception of this act, where have the loans been made, Mr. Speaker?

A total of 280 loans have been made under this legislation for a total amount of $1,273,924. I wonder why this legislation has not met with greater favour among our fishermen? Obviously, our fishermen are a good risk. The report tabled for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1963, shows that since the inception of the act the government has paid only nine claims amounting to $4,543. What other industry, what other lending institution, can boast such a record? I submit this record shows the strong character of our fishermen. It shows their integrity and desire to adhere to a principle or a set of values. It is evident that once a fisherman assumes a financial responsibility it is not something he takes lightly. It is a burden to be carried and a debt to be repaid, even though sometimes it is repaid at great personal sacrifice-a sacrifice he, his wife and family bear.
These facts must be stressed strongly by the minister and should somehow be recognized in a special release from his department. At the very least, these facts should be recognized by the minister when he moves his amendment. It is his stated objective to amend this legislation at a later stage by bringing in a new bill.
The minister has suggested that the amount which may be borrowed should be increased to $25,000; but he said nothing about increasing the time permitted for the repayment of the loan. As a result we, on this side of the house, are prepared to move a subamendment, if necessary, stipulating that the loan shall be repayable in full, according to the terms thereof, in not more than 15 years. A fisherman will not take this extra time to pay if fishing is good and his earnings are high.

The life expectancy of his wooden boat is greater than 15 years. In my view the fisherman ought to be given this extra time if he requires it, in order to meet his payments.
I am pleased the minister has indicated his intention to move a motion at a later date calling for an increase from $10,000 to $25,000 in the amount which can be borrowed. In today's inflated, high cost society, this amount is still not adequate to assist our fishermen in getting established. But even in biblical days, a few loaves and fishes fed the multitude. I suppose it is not necessarily the quantity of material available that matters but the manner in which it is used which is important.
The fisherman will have to work out his own program under the new terms of the loan. We endorse and approve the amendment, even though the minister's methods of promoting the change are rather strange. I say this because this bill received second reading on January 21, 1969. At that time there was no mention in the bill of changing the upper limit of the amount to be borrowed. The measure received second reading and was referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry for clause by clause study. However, in a speech on February 1 in Vancouver the minister had this to say about the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act:
No doubt you will ask me how you, as an individual fisherman, can hope to own your own boat. I will reply by saying that you should take advantage of our new federal Fisheries Improvement Loans Act. This Act, which has recently been updated, is geared to finance loans of up to $25,000. You can borrow up to 75% of the cost of a new boat, or new gear, or a new shore installation. You can borrow up to $25,000 from any bank, or credit union, or insurance company. And you will be able to borrow this money at a lower rate of interest than is available to anyone else in Canada -anyone that is except the Government of Canada itself.

Let me say at once that we agree with the minister and approve of his suggestion that the loan limit be raised. However, we disagree with the kite-flying methods used by this cabinet when endeavouring to establish government policy. For example, the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans), says we should get out of NATO while the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Cadieux) tells the nation that NATO is vitally important to the future protection of this country. At the same time the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), says that neither minister was stating government policy. The minister in charge of housing, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hellyer), states the 11
February 10, 1969

per cent sales tax on construction machinery and building materials should be removed in order to speed up housing development in Canada. At the same time the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has told the house that the sales tax will only be removed over his dead body.
These controversies do not aid our regional problems, do not strengthen our national unity and are obviously put forward by the government to keep the country guessing while they procrastinate on policy. This is what the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) has been doing, procrastinating on policy. While the fisherman waits for a definite policy under the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, the minister goes kite-flying in British Columbia. While the fishermen on the Atlantic coast wait for a program of subsidies which will enable them to improve their fishing fleet, or wait for an indication from the minister with regard to his over-all policy for fisheries development, all we receive from him in reply to questions concerning policy are negative and evasive answers.
Since the diversification of groundfish production became firmly established on the Atlantic coast, seldom in our history have there been occasions when the fishing industry has been so severely or widely threatened. Only three or four species have enabled the industry to remain solvent. Groundfish are being sold today in many instances for less than the cost of production.
In order to avert still more serious dislocations in fishing activity, which will be most difficult to repair once they have occurred, quick action is needed on the part of federal authorities. Constant losses and tightening credit, plus escalating costs for equipment, plus some of the lowest prices in history for groundfish products, have placed our fishermen and producers on the Atlantic coast in a precarious position. Despite all our effort to have the Minister of Fisheries and the government act on this important matter, to date all we have had from the government is a do-nothing, procrastinating attitude. We need action from this government on Canada's territorial seas and fishing zone limits. This act was passed in 1964 and yet we heard today from the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) that discussions and deliberations are still going on with the governments of the United States, France and other countries on this important matter.
The government promised the fishermen during election campaigns in 1962, 1963 and 1964 that this act, when passed, would be

Fisheries Improvement Loans Act implemented by unilateral action. We need action from the government on conservation measures, and this can only be done adequately by calling another conference on the law of the sea. The fisheries industry needs a spokesman at the United Nations to alert other fishing nations to the fact that our resources on our continental shelf are not inexhaustable. When we ask what is being done about this very serious problem, the only reply we receive is that it is under consideration; maybe something will be done next week or next year. When are we going to see something done on these urgent matters?
These are but a few of the urgent matters requiring attention, but I stress them to the Minister of Fisheries and the government in the hope that something will be done. In view of the large area, the large number of fishermen and their families as well as the ancillary industries which are affected by our fisheries, I express the hope this government will take early action to correct some of these problems which are creating serious financial difficulties for the fishing industry of the Atlantic provinces.

Mr. Speaker I rise only because I would like to take a leaf out of your Honour's book and enter a caveat with respect to some of the points that were made by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis). He said that he had consulted the authorities. That is quite a phrase. Sometimes the authorities are people, sometimes they are books, and there are plenty of both.
I agree with the minister when he says that in order to amend this bill in a way that might involve the expenditure of money not envisaged in the bill as it was first presented,

it would be necessary to bring before the house the approval of the Governor General. But when he says that he cannot amend this bill, which is a bill to amend the original act, by adding to it other amendments to the original act I think he had better go back and discuss that with the authorities again. As a matter of fact, I suggest to him that he might be in even greater difficulty bringing in a second bill in the same session amending the original act than he would be by trying to get some amendments incorporated into this bill. It all depends on what he does.
He says that the amendments in his new bill will not be amendments to this bill, that they will be amendments to the original act. But if there is any inconsistency or any conflict I suggest he could be in the same kind of trouble that our friend Jack Pickersgill got into on one occasion. I would remind the minister that there have been occasions when bills that had already been presented and started were amended beyond what was originally intended. It used to be that this meant going beyond the terms of the resolution preceding a bill. We have done away with that, but we still have to consider the intention of the bill as agreed to by the Governor General.
For example, I think of the medicare bill which had written into it a clause having to do with other than medical services. At first, it was argued that this could not be put into the bill because it was not part of the original intention. But when the government finally did do it, it did so by bringing in another recommendation from the Governor General. There was the Canada Pension Plan, and I remember once or twice that Mr. Garson did this kind of thing in the days when he was here. I am sure there are other examples of this, where matters that were germaine to the general subject were brought into the amending bill before the house.
As I say, I think it would be less difficult to amend this bill by adding something else, as long as you get the approval of the Governor General, than it will be to bring in a second bill in the same session amending an act on the statute books. Frankly, I think the suggestion made by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding) is the best one. The minister should let this bill stand or ask that it be withdrawn and bring in a completely new bill incorporating the things in this bill that he wants and the other proposals that he would like to make.
I do not raise this as a point of order, Mr. Speaker. Indeed, the minister did not present

his arguments as a point of order but I felt that I for one could not let his remarks go unchallenged as though they were the gospel. As you know, the gospel, can be according to various authorities, and I think this might well have to be looked into.
I would urge the minister to consider asking that this bill be withdrawn, or at least asking that it stand, and that he bring in a completely new bill, so we will have one bill at this session making all the amendments that he wants to make to the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act.

HOUSING-PROVISIONS TO ASSIST LOW INCOME CANADIANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, ten days ago I quoted the opinion of the Canadian Welfare Council that the report of the Hellyer task force on housing includes no proposals to help the one million Canadians with annual incomes under $5,500. I asked the minister what other proposals he had to provide housing for these people. Tonight, I ask him the same question, or whomever he has delegated to answer.
I am not denying that there are some good proposals in the report but they are proposals that would help the upper income levels of our population. The decision to cold storage
February 10, 1969
5360	COMMONS DEBATES
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion public housing and urban renewal is a shocking betrayal of those who most need help, those who cannot possibly provide homes by their own efforts. Up to now the government has discriminated in favour of those best able to provide houses for themselves. What we need now is government discrimination in favour of the lower income half. I refer to the elderly, the single parent families, the great group headed by women with dependant children, employed people whose wages will not allow them to buy a home under any circumstances or even rent one that is not a firetrap, a rat trap, or both. The method of attacking existing public housing projects for their bad features does not provide an excuse for failing to build good, modern ones. In a second brief presented to the task force on November 29 last, the mayor and council of my own city said:
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
The city ol Vancouver is extremely concerned at any suggestion that the federal government withdraw or in any way limit its involvement in urban renewal schemes. On the contrary, it is the city's view that such involvement must be increased.
While the brief states that there has been a reaction against the concentration of low income and welfare recipients into areas stigmatized as "ghettos", and while admitting that the idea of public housing has not yet been accepted by all communities, nevertheless, the brief suggests:
-the city feels very strongly that public housing, as presently contemplated, is one way of accommodating those people who are economically unable to provide for their housing needs.
The federal task force has failed the city of Vancouver. It has failed the people of Vancouver, thousands of them, who need housing and cannot get it on their own. It has failed the people of every city across Canada who are in the same miserable dilemma. By seeing only home owners and potential home owners, by raising the N.H.A. mortgage limit to $35,000, by proposing to remove the interest ceiling altogether, the minister has ensured that housing for the upper income half will continue to be the aim of government policy.
The New Democratic party urges the federal government to begin with the needs of the two thirds of Canadian families whose annual incomes are below $7,500. Public housing? Yes. Rent supplements? Yes, if accompanied by a program of rent controls and the enforcement of local housing codes. This, of course, means co-operation with provincial
[Mrs. Maclnnis (Vancouver-Kingsway) j
governments. Why not? The task force was composed of a distinguished group of academics with a sprinkling of practical builders and a strong-minded politician. I wish it had taken time to look at the report of the guidelines committee of the Canadian conference on housing held in Toronto last October, which said:
Canadian housing goals will not be easy to achieve. They require much higher priority within the public economy (federal and provincial) and should be seen to be as socially essential as education. No government is spending according to the priorities this conference insists on.
As long as government allocations for housing are insufficient, priority within housing budgets should go to helping those with the greatest need-
And those last two words are underlined.
-including ethnic minorities, regional areas and poverty groups, whether through housing policies or through employment and income policies.
I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, that the hard working and comfortable task force has turned this advice upside down. It has provided a blueprint that helps those best able to help themselves.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer to my question the other day the minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows that the answer to that is no.
I will overlook the somewhat presumptuous flippancy of the reply and ask how I could possibly know his answer would be in the negative, having noted some very definite and distinct changes he has made in respect of such things as the five day delivery in rural areas, the imposition of the five day delivery in the rest of the country and having noted the number of quick turns some of his colleagues like the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) have had to make in certain important areas. We are all aware of the increasing protests from publishers of all kinds of important publications in respect of the drastic increase which will soon be imposed upon them.
I was interested in the comment of the leader of the N.D.P. in Ontario. I do not believe in the organ in question and I am reasonably sure I would disagree with most of the information it disseminates. But political parties are essential to a democracy, and they must be able to communicate with the citizenry.
Not long ago two large and important national organizations, even larger than the N.D.P., stated their views and disappointment in this matter. The Canadian Federation of Agriculture on February 3 passed a unanimous resolution on postal rates. This resolution on postal rates asked the government not to implement, as presently worded, Bill C-116 raising postal rates for newspapers and periodicals. The resolution also indicated that the impact of this bill on farm publications would result in increased mailing costs ranging between 230 per cent and 2,000 per cent. It pointed out that the farm press was a vital tool in farm production and management, since it kept farmers informed of technological innovations.
On the same day the Canadian Labour Congress dealt with the same question. Let me read from a Canadian Press release on this matter:
The Canadian Labour Congress has accused the federal government of curtailing freedom of expression by imposing what the C.L.C. terms exorbitant postal rates for non-profit publications.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
William Dodge, C.L.C. secretary-treasurer, said yesterday several trade union publications may have to cease publication because of increased postal rates scheduled for April 1.
The article then continues:
Mr. Dodge said the postal rate increase threatens freedom of expression because the printed word is the only effective way a union or a similar organization has of reaching its members. He said the increase would also result in the loss of employment in the printing industry, pulp and paper and related fields.
The article then states:
Mr. Dodge said the Canadian Brotherhood of Railway, Transport and General Workers estimates that its postal bill for its bi-monthly, Canadian Transport, will climb from $1,057 to $29,696. The international association of machinists has estimated that the cost of mailing its weekly, The Machinist, will go up from $9,024 to $99,840.
These increases are absolutely phenomenal and the portents are painful, indeed. We have been told by these people that there is a great danger that Canadian publications will have to bow out and we will find the Canadian unions having to put up with United States publications in their fields. As one of the editors said, it is ironic that after years of fighting for independent Canadian union papers we may lose them now because of measures taken by our own government.
It is a serious thing that so many important groups in our society will have their capacity for communication so drastically curtailed. There is one other aspect involved and that is competition with United States publications which Canadian post offices will still have to carry. This process will not help the minister much in his deficit fighting activity.
I can think of another type of competition; that is competition from government departments. Will the organs of organized labour in Canada be forced out of business by the exorbitant rates? Will the publications of the Department of Labour go through the mails easier?
To take another example, will publications of institutes of international affairs and like groups have to be diminished or curtailed while External Affairs, the journal of the Department of External Affairs, goes out with regularity and ease? One can imagine the amount of critical content on government policy which the department's publication will include! I doubt, indeed, if the minister's speeches on NATO will ever find their way into this slick magazine.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I am not complaining about the free use of mails for such purposes. A government

5362	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion should be able to communicate with its people, and vice versa. The franking privilege works both ways, and so it should. But a government should not have a monopoly or a near-monopoly on the communication of ideas and information on any aspect of public policy or national interest. Therein lies the danger.
I join the many organizations, groups and individuals who have appealed to us, and I am sure they must be appealing to the minister every day, if not every hour on the hour, to take another look at the ramifications which will stem from the imposition of the legislation and to look at the whole question of the communication of ideas of important groups within this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this question and this type of proposal has been answered on many occasions in the past. I will only refer to the example of the Canadian Labour Congress. They have submitted a brief to the government and will be presenting it later this month. They have made reference to the increase in postal rates. I will then repeat publicly what I have already told Mr. Dodge and others privately:	I admit that the
increases, on a percentage basis, appear to be and are, in fact, substantial. On the other hand, when one breaks down the increases into a cost per subscription per year, in fact it is very minor indeed.
In a long letter which I wrote to Mr. Dodge with respect to 11 major journals, the editors of which met with me in my office, I stated that in most cases the figure was about 30 cents, 40 cents or 50 cents per annum. An increase of this order for weeklies or bimonthlies would cover the entire increases in the postage rates, as astronomical as they may appear to be when cited in absolute terms by my hon. colleague. In other words, Mr. Speaker, this is all relative. What is not relative is the fact that the Post Office would have operated at a deficit of $130 million this year; that by changing the philosophy of the Post Office and charging those who use its services on the basis of user cost and not on the basis of indirect subsidy by the government, we are accomplishing a great deal.
By far the greatest impact will be felt in the business sector. These are the people who use the mails the most, and they will be paying for it. What do we accomplish if we reduce that deficit from $130 million to about $30 million? The government will have $100 million to spend on other priorities, whether


they be in the field of increasing its armed forces, education, regional development, putting satellites into the sky, or any other program.

maintopic: POST OFFICE DEPARTMENT-DISPUTE WITH LETTER CARRIERS UNION-DOWNWARD RATES REVISION
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Harding).

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I asked the Postmaster General (Mr. Kierans) whether his department had reviewed the decision which he made last fall to increase Post Office box rentals. His reply was in the negative. I must agree that some of the postal rates on mail, etc. were in need of adjusting. However, I am not only opposed to the increase in the post office box rentals but feel that they should have been eliminated altogether. This Liberal administration talks about a just society. I certainly believe in this concept, but I do not support the fact that nearly every move made by the present administration is in the opposite direction. The increase in post office box rentals is a small but a good example of injustice. One would imagine that within the Post Office Department there would be no discrimination so far as the main services were concerned. This is not so, for we see in our smaller centres and in rural areas a clear cut case of discrimination when charges are made to the local residents for the privilege of having their sorted mail placed in a post office box. In the larger urban areas the mail is delivered to the residences and no extra charge is made for this service.
Mail arrives at their homes free of charge and this service, which the urban areas have and need, is paid for out of the general post office revenues. In the smaller communities, however, there is no delivery to the homes. The residents are forced to go to a central location for their mail. This is both time consuming and costly. In addition, if they wish to obtain their mail after regular post office hours, they must rent a post office box or do without their daily mail. If those living in the urban areas can have a free delivery service to their homes, the least the postal department can do for those in the smaller centres
February 10. 1969
is to give them free use of post office boxes. This would be one way of bringing a greater degree of justice to our mail service.
I understand the Postmaster General's desire to increase the revenues of his department. The former box rentals were discriminatory because the small centres were forced to pay for this service when the larger areas were receiving free delivery. Today, this unjust cost to the residents of the smaller centres has been compounded by the sharp increase in box rentals everywhere. I again protest this increase on behalf of many of my constituents.
I would like to pose several questions for the minister's consideration and, I hope, reply. Is it not cheaper for the post office to put the mail in boxes than to deliver it? The answer obviously is, yes. Then, as one of my constituents put it, why do we have to pay for an inferior postal box service when the home delivery is free? It irks me to see the sharp increase in post office box rentals. We are told the increases must help to pay the cost of operating this facet of postal service. At the same time we know that two U.S. magazines, Time and Reader's Digest, pay only about one third of their total mailing costs.
The Canadian public subsidizes the mailing costs of these publications to the extent of just over $1J million. In view of this type of subsidization of non-Canadians, I again urge the minister to review his position on post office box rentals and, for a first move, to roll the rents back to the old level finally, he could eliminate these charges to bring a little more justice to those who are forced to use these boxes. Let us make all our moves in the right direction to bring about a just society.

Mr. Speaker, there are several ways of answering this question. In the first place I would like to point out the fact that there has been no change whatsoever in the rates for the rental of post office boxes since the year 1927.
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion (10:20 p.m.)
Obviously, the cost has increased a great deal since then. We are not making any profit on this service; we are indeed losing on it, but we are trying to lose less than we did. The people in small communities where these facilities are available are not being discriminated against. They can get their mail free, just as anyone in a large city or on a rural route. In these small post offices they can get it at a general delivery wicket, and a great many of them choose to do this. On the other hand, in these small communities there are businessmen, professional people, families, who prefer to take advantage of an additional facility. Boxes are therefore made available to them as an additional service. In other words, they have a choice, no matter where they are, of getting mail free on general delivery or of engaging boxes which will enable them to collect mail at any time convenient, and enjoy many other advantages besides.
In other words, the boxes are available at all times, as is the general delivery. Rural route and urban deliveries are made once a day. I think I should repeat once again my reply to the charge, which is always intermingled with whatever valid criticism is made, that we are discriminating in favour of two United States magazines. We are not. The subsidy granted to these magazines is part of what has been granted to the magazine industry. We are not discriminating either against them or in their favour.
I do not know what else there is to be said about this question. We are trying to operate on the basis that those who use our services should pay for them. The less we need to subsidize services for which the government can legitimately charge, the less will be the tax burden on the Canadian people or, alternatively, the more the government will be able to do to satisfy other public needs.
